12805-the-boy-allies-in-the-balkan-campa:
Clair W. Hayes sent his Boy Allies, Hal Paine and Chester Crawford, to the Balkans in this 1916 war adventure. The story opens in the air at dawn, with a sick passenger named Stubbs begging to get back to earth, while Hal guides their military aeroplane. Battles, escapes, and a struggle to save a nation follow.

Hand-to-hand fights, including a wrestling bout where Nicolas drops Ivan by the legs, give the action its punch. The boys move between armies, spies, and mountain roads in the series' brisk style. Young readers of the war years got here a stirring, if simple, Balkan tale.
20549-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris wrote his Historic Tales series to bring the past alive as story, and this ninth volume, published in 1908, covers Scandinavia. It retells the history and legends of Sweden, Norway, and Denmark. Kings, vikings, and heroes fill its pages.

One tale reaches back to the days of the early legends. Many centuries ago, the book says, there reigned over Uppsala in Sweden a king named Erik. He had no son and only one daughter, but this girl was worth a dozen sons and daughters of other men. Morris aimed such tales at family reading, history with the blood still in it.
21841-the-saddle-boys-in-the-grand-canyo:
Frank Haywood lifts his glasses on a canyon trail in this Saddle Boys adventure by Captain James Carson, published in 1913. His friend Bob Archer, a Kentucky lad, rides beside him. A wolf pack's work opens the tale, and a floating bottle starts the mystery. Soon the boys are bound for the Grand Canyon itself, with their horse Buckskin standing guard along the way.

A hermit in a cave waits at the heart of the canyon country. Chapters bring a listener under a window, a stand for the law, and a Moqui caught napping. Carson wrote the series for boys who loved the range. It is western series fiction at full gallop: scenery, danger, and two steady lads.
26081-fighting-the-traffic-in-young-girl:
Ernest A. Bell's 1910 exposé attacks the traffic in young girls, which he calls the greatest crime in the world's history. Chapters trace the trade from Babylon, Greece, and Rome to the modern city, then set out how procurers coax girls away and deliver them to dive-keepers. Ice cream parlors and fruit stores appear as common first traps.

Bell prints poems, pictures, and an introduction by Edwin W. Sims, and he charges that police often return escaped girls to the dives or send them to prison instead of helping them. The book ends as a call to action, urging readers and officials to break the trade and protect girls before they are drawn in.
32746-the-revival-of-irish-literature-ad:
Sir Charles Gavan Duffy, George Sigerson, and Douglas Hyde address the Irish Literary Society in London in this 1894 volume. Duffy speaks in July 1892 and June 1893 on what Irishmen may do for Irish literature and on books for the Irish people. Sigerson traces the origin and setting of that literature, and Hyde urges the de-Anglicising of Ireland.

Duffy recalls a fruitful age before the famine of 1846, when young writers dug up buried history and sang songs of valor and hope. Famine, prison, and exile broke their work, yet it fed two generations. The speakers call for Irish books, Irish speech, and a place for Irish in public exams.
34394-the-boy-scouts-of-bob-s-hill-a-seq:
The Boy Scouts of Bob's Hill, by Charles Pierce Burton, continues the Bob's Hill tales. Its front pages list the officers of the Boy Scouts of America. Woodrow Wilson stands as honorary president. Theodore Roosevelt and William Taft stand as honorary vice-presidents. Ernest Thompson Seton is named chief scout, and Daniel Carter Beard national commissioner. A letter from national headquarters, dated July 31, 1913, speaks to the public. Scout leaders, it says, learned that boys are won in their leisure hours.

At such times tales of daring capture the boy, the letter argues. Taste should be trained, not thwarted. Cheap tales were spoiling that taste, the board warns. Books the boy likes best, yet books best for the boy, were the aim. The story that follows carries that badge into fiction.
40830-twenty-five-years-in-a-waggon-in-s:
Andrew Anderson spent Twenty-Five Years in a Waggon in South Africa, and his book joins sport and travel in one long trek. In his preface he states his object, to add another page to the physical geography of Africa. The region he chose for his travels had been an unknown land on all maps of the dark interior, as he puts it.

Anderson hunted, traded, and mapped from the Cape toward the Zambesi in the years when wagons were the only ships of the veldt. Lions, elephants, fever, and thirst share his road with fine scenery and strange peoples. His maps served those who came after. Readers get a quarter century of African wagon life from a steady, observant pioneer.
43795-sketches-of-central-asia-1868-addi:
Arminius Vambery, professor of Oriental languages at the University of Pesth, wrote Sketches of Central Asia, published at Philadelphia and London in 1868. The book adds chapters on his travels, adventures, and the ethnology of Central Asia. His preface answers reviewers of his Travels in Central Asia. They had reproached him with scantiness of detail and scrappiness of treatment. They said he had said much less than he could about his journey.

Vambery had crossed Central Asia in disguise as a dervish, reaching Khiva, Bokhara, and Samarkand when few Europeans could. This volume adds the peoples, tongues, and customs the first book had slighted. It remains a first-hand window on a closed region.
44038-through-the-yukon-gold-diggings-a-:
Through the Yukon Gold Diggings is a narrative of personal travel by Josiah Edward Spurr. Spurr went north as a geologist of the United States Geological Survey in charge. His party was the first expedition that department sent into the interior of Alaska. Eastern Publishing of Boston issued the narrative in 1900 with a flannel shirt frontispiece.

His charge was to study the Yukon gold diggings, then vague news to the world. A government report on the geology of the district carried his formal results. The Klondike discovery broke while he travelled the mining regions of the north. Readers gain both science and adventure from a survey man on the ground.
45381-the-popular-story-of-blue-beard-em:
Anonymous hands shaped this cheap story book of Blue Beard, dressed with neat engravings. Long ago and far from any town, a rich man lived in a fine castle on a rise, ringed by groves. His rooms hung with damask, his chairs wore velvet fringed with gold, and his plates were silver and gold. His coaches might have served a king.

Yet his face was fierce and his beard a frightful blue, and the country round called him Blue Beard in fear. Word said he had wed many fair ladies, and no one could tell what became of them. Two sisters, Anne and Fatima, shrink from his offer of marriage at first word of it. The old tale of the locked room follows.
52227-piece-goods-manual-fabrics-describ:
Blanco, a second assistant in the Chinese Maritime Customs, compiled this trade manual, printed at Shanghai in 1917 by the customs printing office. The catalog title is a stray line of the subtitle; the book is the Piece Goods Manual. It was made to help customs men name and class the cloth samples that passed through Chinese ports.

The pages describe fabrics one by one, covering woven goods and knit goods. Weaving terms are explained in plain words, and notes tell how samples should be classed for duty. Drawings help the officer match a sample to its name. The manual is a working tool of the old treaty port trade, and it preserves the cloth vocabulary of its day.
56562-kidnapped-illustrated-being-memoir:
Robert Louis Stevenson's Kidnapped tells the adventures of David Balfour in the year 1751. Cheated by his uncle Ebenezer Balfour of Shaws, David is kidnapped aboard a brig, cast away on a desert isle, and thrown among Highland Jacobites after the Appin murder. His friend and foil is Alan Breck Stewart, the fiery Highlander with whom he crosses the wild Highlands.

Scribner published this illustrated edition at New York in 1946, with pictures by Wyeth. Stevenson's dedication, addressed to Charles Baxter, jokes about the liberties he took with the Appin murder and the map, and owns the book was written for the winter evening schoolroom. It is one of the great adventure novels in English, part history and part boy's tale of escape and pursuit.
62480-above-the-french-lines-letters-of-:
Above the French Lines holds the letters of Stuart Walcott, American aviator, from July 4, 1917, to December 8, 1917. Princeton University Press printed the book in April 1918. A photo shows Walcott in his aeroplane at the front. His father wrote a short life note at the close.

The contents run from Princeton to France, then the letters, then The Final Combat. Plates show Walcott at the front and his War Cross with Palm, given in honor of his service. The life note says Benjamin Stuart Walcott was of New England ancestry. His earliest known American forbear was Captain Jonathan Walcott of Salem, Massachusetts, who lived from 1663 to 1699. The letters thus end in a death in action over France. War readers get a young flier whole war in his own hand.
64785-the-spanish-influenza-pandemic-of-:
The Spanish Influenza Pandemic of 1918, an account of its ravages in Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, records how one county met the great flu epidemic. Its front pages carry a certificate of merit for the physicians, nurses, Red Cross workers, and volunteers of the county.

The certificate honors people who gave time, health, and in several cases their lives to nurse the stricken during the world epidemic. Local accounts like this one were printed across the country after 1918, naming helpers and tallying loss while memory was raw. The book stands as both a medical record and a memorial to civilian courage in a plague year.
67358-the-thousand-buddhas-ancient-buddh:
The Thousand Buddhas describes ancient Buddhist paintings from the cave-temples of Tun-huang. Aurel Stein recovered the paintings on China's western frontier. He describes them in the text. Laurence Binyon wrote an introductory essay. Bernard Quaritch published the album in London in 1921.

The book appeared under the orders of the India Office. The trustees of the British Museum co-operated. Binyon's essay places the paintings in Buddhist art. Stein's account then treats the pictures one by one. Paradises of several Buddhas come first. Many entries treat forms of Avalokitesvara, the compassionate one. Others treat scenes from the Buddha's life. Banners, paper pictures, and an embroidery close the list.
69090-a-dissuasion-to-great-britain-and-:
A Dissuasion to Great-Britain and the Colonies, from the Slave Trade to Africa was written by James Swan. Swan was a native of Britain living in America, and E Russell printed the tract in Boston. He argues that the African slave trade contradicts divine law. It also contradicts the laws of the provinces themselves.

His title page promises to show the trade's disadvantages for all parties. It promises the gains of ending it for Europe, Africa, Britain, and the plantations. It also explains how trade with Africa could stand on a just and lawful footing instead. In his dedication to all friends of liberty, Swan asks readers to judge with open minds. He begs them not to brand him a Tory for his birth. The tract is an early American print in the long campaign against the trade.
69166-a-short-sketch-of-the-evidence-for:
A Short Sketch of the Evidence for the Abolition of the Slave Trade is a pamphlet first printed at London and reprinted at Philadelphia in 1792. It sums up evidence delivered before a committee of the House of Commons. A note to readers commends the subject to the serious attention of people in general. Its motto is the golden rule, to do to others as you would have them do to you.

The sketch says it does not aim to replace larger works on the trade. It hopes instead to spread their reach and strengthen their effect. Earlier writers, it notes, had been flatly denied and accused of slander. Now a body of solid evidence existed that readers could see and judge for themselves. The pamphlet belongs to the great public campaign against the slave trade. It carried sworn facts to ordinary readers on both sides of the Atlantic.
70309-songs-of-the-slav:
Songs of the Slav holds translations from the Czecho Slovak by Otto Kotouc, printed in Boston by the Poet Lore Company under a 1919 copyright. Five poets stand in the book. The versions were made in the United States, at the Gorham Press.

Jan Kollar opens with the Daughter of Slava. Vitezslav Halek Evening Songs and Svatopluk Cech Songs of the Slave follow. Petr Bezruc holds One Melody, Silesian Forests, a Red Blossom, You and I, and 70,000. J S Machar closes with On Golgotha, a Fantastic Ballad, and sonnets of the past and of life. Kollar sonnet calls a hundred times over to the divided Slavonians. Let us be a whole and not a part in clans, he cries, be one in harmony or naught at all. Verse fans get a new nation poetry in English dress.
britannica-1911-carus-karl-gustav:
Karl Gustav Carus (1789–1869) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a German physiologist and psychologist who was also known as an art critic and landscape painter. Born and educated at Leipzig, he turned to medicine in 1811 and chose comparative anatomy as his lecture subject, a field no one had taught at Leipzig before. He directed a military hospital in the war of 1813 and became professor at the new medical college in Dresden in 1814.

Carus spent the rest of his life in Dresden, becoming royal physician in 1827 and privy councillor in 1862. In philosophy he followed Schelling, and that spirit runs through his work. He treated inherited tendency as proof that the cell holds a kind of psychic life. His chief books include the outlines of comparative anatomy and physiology of 1828 and Psyche, on the history of the soul's development, in 1846.
britannica-1911-cohn-gustav:
Gustav Cohn (born 1840) was a German economist born at Marienwerder in West Prussia on 12 December 1840. He studied at Berlin and Jena. In 1869 he took a post at the polytechnic in Riga. In 1875 he was chosen as professor at the polytechnic at Zürich. A study trip to England in 1873 shaped a key book.

That book treated English railway policy and appeared in 1874 and 1875. In 1884 Cohn became professor of political science at Göttingen. His best known works fill the rest of the entry. They include a system of political economy from 1885 and a work on finance from 1889. Studies in economics came in 1886. A history and politics of transport followed in 1900. The entry is a plain record of posts and books.
britannica-1911-freytag-gustav:
Gustav Freytag (1816-1895), German novelist, was born at Kreuzburg in Silesia on 13 July 1816. He studied philology at Breslau and Berlin, taught at Breslau from 1839, and turned to the stage, winning a lasting place with the comedy Die Journalisten in 1853. From 1848 he co-edited Die Grenzboten, which became the leading voice of German and Austrian liberalism.

His novel Soll und Haben of 1855 was translated into nearly every European language and made his name abroad, praising the German middle class as the soundest part of the nation. Die verlorene Handschrift followed in 1864, and his five-volume Bilder aus der deutschen Vergangenheit pictured German life across the ages. From 1872 he built Die Ahnen, a chain of historical novels following one family to modern times. He rode with the Prussian crown prince staff in 1870 and died at Wiesbaden in April 1895.
britannica-1911-fulleborn-georg-gustav:
Fulleborn, Georg Gustav (1769–1803), a German author and scholar, was born at Glogau on the 2nd of March 1769 and died at Breslau on the 6th of February 1803. He studied at Halle and became professor of classics and philosophy at the Elisabeth gymnasium in Breslau. His Beiträge zur Geschichte der Philosophie helped make the systems of the ancient philosophers known to German readers.

He also wrote an Encyclopaedia philologica in 1798 and a manual on rhetoric. Under the pen name Edelwald Justus he published popular tales drawn from Silesian folk stories, alongside a drama and lighter writings.
britannica-1911-hotho-heinrich-gustav:
Heinrich Gustav Hotho (1802–1873) was a German historian of art, born at Berlin in 1802. Measles left him blind for two years in boyhood, but he recovered his sight and studied so hard that he took his degree at Berlin in 1826. A year of travel through Paris, London and the Low Countries fixed his calling. He came home delighted with the art he had seen.

Hotho passed as docent in aesthetics and art history, and in 1829 became professor at Berlin university. In 1833 Waagen took him as assistant in the Prussian capital's museum. In 1858 he rose to direct its print-room. His time split between writing and official duties for a long, busy life. His ambition was always to master the schools of Germany and the Netherlands, and most of what he published kept to those fields. He died in his native city on Christmas day 1873.
doe-osti-3000129-low-temperature-cyclic-:
Qizhen Li of Washington State University wrote this final report for award DE-SC0016333 on how the lightest structural metal tires. Magnesium weighs less than any rival structural metal, so car and aircraft parts made from it save fuel. Yet magnesium's hexagonal crystal packing gives it unusual slip and twinning behaviour, and parts under repeated loading can fail by fatigue in ways designers still cannot fully predict, especially in the cold.

The project bent ultrafine-grained pure magnesium back and forth at low temperatures and watched the damage build. Processing routes that refine the grain structure were explored alongside, to see how they shift strength and fatigue life. Results appeared in journal articles and talks at TMS, MRS and plasticity conferences. The work serves both alloy designers and the wider public case for magnesium in passenger vehicles: lighter cars, better fuel economy, lower emissions.
doe-osti-3816579-local-air-quality-impac:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-6A20-98560, dated September 2026, models the air quality cost of a peak-shaving diesel generator in Waynesville, North Carolina. Vikram Ravi and Garvin Heath are the printed authors. The town's diesel unit fires on high-demand days to trim peak power buys. Each run sends out fine particles, sulfur dioxide, and carbon monoxide. The study asks where that plume lands and what it means for nearby lungs.

Emission rates were built from standard factors for diesel engines. A puff model named SCICHEM tracked the plume hour by hour over local terrain and weather. Outputs map peak particle levels and plume spread, and a health layer turns levels into harm estimates. The work sits inside the Communities LEAP assistance program. It gives town leaders a grounded view of a trade-off judged by price alone.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KairysDavidRudo: Harold Weisberg wrote to David Kairys and David Rudovsky on May 1, 1976. Both men were lawyers known for civil liberties work, the kind of counsel a records litigant would write to. The archive's entry names the parties and the date but gives nothing of the letter's substance. It stands as a single dated letter in Weisberg's legal correspondence.
nasa-tm-19640017334-on-the-structure-of-: Two Goddard Space Flight Center authors wrote this February 1964 paper on the structure of a collision-free wave in a plasma. The wave runs across a magnetic field, as the title states. Plasma is hot, charged gas, and collision-free waves cross it without particles striking each other. The hosted sample preserves only the report's title page, with no readable abstract or body text, so its analysis cannot be described from the sample itself.
nasa-tm-19700026442-an-empirical-techniq:
The Mathematical Physics Branch at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston issued this internal note on June 2, 1969. It gives a practical technique for computing navigation covariance matrices. Such matrices state how unsure a spacecraft's known position is, and planners needed honest figures for lunar orbit flights after Apollo 8.

The technique rests on real postflight tracking work from Apollo 8 and Lunar Orbiter III. Those flights showed the Moon's gravity field was known less well than planners had assumed. Measured errors in chosen orbit values feed the method, which then produces the expected navigation accuracy. Applied to Missions F and G, it modeled the slow growth of down-track position errors well.
the-boy-allies-in-the-balkan-campaign-or:
Clair W. Hayes wrote The Boy Allies in the Balkan Campaign, or The Struggle to Save a Nation, dated 1916. The first chapter is called In the Air. It opens in a war aeroplane at dawn, high and cold. Hal Paine flies the craft, with three riders behind him.

One of those riders, Mr. Stubbs, sits curled in a ball and groans at times. When Hal asks how he feels, Stubbs says he is sick. He asks how long it will be till they land, so he may die in peace. Hal laughs and tells him he will not die. Chester Crawford, Hal's close friend, asks where they are. Hal, eyes fixed ahead, says they are somewhere over Central Austria. The first light grows in the east as they fly on.
